reason: The court held that the guarantors had renounced excussion and were liable as principal debtors, so the quote supports a dispositive suretyship rule with no statute claimed.
The no-advice/no-warranty holding was necessary to dismiss the counterclaim, but the supporting quote is a quotation from another case rather than this court's own holding.
The quoted passage states the ordinary benefit of excussion, but the court's actual holding was that this benefit had been waived by the guarantors.
The court held that section 7 and a three-year period applied, while the quote is from Silva v Silva and the statement confusingly suggests a one-year goods-sold rule.
The court accepted the instalment-purchase document as residence proof in the special circumstances under a school circular, not as a rule construing Prevention of Frauds Ordinance section 4.
The court expressly applied the Polluter Pays principle to order the 8th respondent to fund compensation and rehabilitation, with no statute section claimed.
The court held that a public officer must receive sufficient grounds for a transfer to exercise the constitutional appeal right, and the quote directly supports that holding.
The court held the exigencies-of-service transfer arbitrary because Clause 218 criteria and the real reasons were not properly disclosed to the officer.
The transfer reasoning is materially tied to PSC Rules 218 and 221 and Article 12, while the cited Evidence Ordinance section 114(f) was only an evidential inference point.
The extracted rule overstates a borrowed Doody formulation as an absolute rule, whereas this court's holding was the narrower fair-hearing breach in the gem-licence process.
The malpractice standard was applied to remove the attorney, but the supporting quote is a passage from In Re Arthenayake rather than this court's own formulation.
The eight-year suspension was the order, but the quote does not support that rule and section 19(2) only governed notarial disqualification after attorney suspension.
The quoted expectation of high standards was stated by the court, but the holding discharged the rule after finding no deceit or malpractice in the particular circumstances.
